title: Kubernetes Multi-Cluster Project Karmada Reaches CNCF Graduation
gist: Karmada, a multi-cluster and multi-cloud Kubernetes orchestration project, reached CNCF graduation at KubeCon China 2026 alongside a v1.19 release that improves multi-component scheduling for AI training jobs, positioning it as the production successor to the archived KubeFed as GPU capacity fragments across regions and clouds.

themes.theme: GPU scarcity is driving multi-cluster orchestration

insights.claim: As GPU capacity is spread across regions and cloud providers, no single Kubernetes cluster holds enough accelerators, so distributed AI training and inference workloads must be split, scheduled and shifted across many systems.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Accelerator scarcity is the structural reason multi-cluster orchestration is moving from niche to mandatory infrastructure.
insights.quote: No single cluster has enough accelerators.

insights.claim: The graduation release, v1.19, enhances multi-component scheduling for AI training jobs and promotes priority-based scheduling to Beta with the feature on by default.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: The project's roadmap has visibly reoriented around AI workloads rather than generic hybrid-cloud failover.

insights.claim: Adopters use the project for GPU/CPU scheduling for AI workloads alongside hybrid cloud capacity, cross-region resilience and fleet-wide configuration distribution, showing AI is now one of several converging drivers.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Multi-cluster demand has multiple independent drivers, which makes it durable rather than an AI-cycle artifact.

insights.claim: Karmada builds on the standard Kubernetes API rather than replacing it, so existing manifests, controllers and tools work unchanged on its control plane.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Zero-migration compatibility is the decisive adoption lever, and it is exactly what the predecessor project lacked.
insights.quote: It doesn’t replace it, so existing manifests, controllers, and tools work without changes on a Karmada control plane.

insights.claim: The earlier approach to running one app across multiple clusters required custom automation or the now-archived KubeFed project, which forced teams to learn a different federated-resources API and suffered flexibility problems.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: The failure mode of the prior generation was API divergence, a lesson that generalises to any platform abstraction layer.

insights.claim: Placement logic is expressed through two custom APIs: a PropagationPolicy mapping one policy to many workloads with cluster affinity, splitting/rebalancing and multi-dimension HA across region, availability zone, cluster or provider, and an OverridePolicy that rewrites cluster-specific configuration without touching the resource template.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Separating placement policy from resource templates is the reusable mental model for any fleet-scale configuration problem.

insights.claim: An OverridePolicy can swap container image prefixes by region or StorageClass by cloud provider, which is the concrete mechanism that makes a single workload definition portable across competing clouds.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Cloud-specific lock-in points are being abstracted into policy, weakening provider differentiation at the platform layer.

insights.claim: The control plane comprises a Karmada API Server, Controller Manager and Scheduler backed by its own etcd instance for state, effectively a Kubernetes-shaped control plane layered above member clusters.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Running a second etcd-backed control plane is a real operational cost buyers must weigh against fleet management benefits.

insights.claim: Four controllers perform propagation: a Cluster Controller for member lifecycle, a Policy Controller binding matching resources into ResourceBinding objects, a Binding Controller turning bindings into per-cluster Work objects, and an Execution Controller pushing manifests to each member cluster's API server.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: The push-based propagation chain is what determines blast radius and failure behaviour in a fleet rollout.

insights.claim: Karmada exports Prometheus metrics from its control-plane components and ships Helm charts, plugging into existing CNCF observability and deployment tooling instead of requiring a separate stack.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Reusing the incumbent observability stack lowers the operational objection to adopting another control plane.

insights.claim: Since joining the CNCF Sandbox in September 2021 and moving to Incubating in December 2023, the project has grown to over 1,214 contributors from 292 organizations and more than 5,600 GitHub stars.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: A roughly five-year sandbox-to-graduation arc with 292 contributing organizations is the benchmark for CNCF project maturity timelines.

insights.claim: Production adopters include Bloomberg, Wellhub, Alibaba Cloud, Huawei, Trip.com, Bilibili, iFLYTEK, JDCloud, Kuaishou, RedNote, SenseTime, Vivo, WPS and ZTO, a roster heavily weighted toward Chinese hyperscale internet firms.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: The project's centre of gravity is Chinese hyperscalers, which shapes both its roadmap priorities and its geopolitical adoption profile in Western enterprises.

insights.claim: Graduation required a third-party security audit, a formal steering committee, adoption of the CNCF Code of Conduct and maintenance of a CII Best Practices Badge.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: These are the concrete governance gates any project must clear before enterprises treat it as procurement-safe.

insights.claim: A Trip.com senior development expert reports operating multiple clusters as a unified resource pool with cross-cluster elasticity, failover and large-scale workload migration at minimal disruption, without changing existing Kubernetes resource definitions.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: A named production reference at scale is the evidence enterprises look for before fleet-level bets.
insights.quote: it has enabled us to operate multiple clusters as a unified resource pool, support cross-cluster elasticity and failover

insights.claim: The project's TOC sponsor frames the value proposition as consistent management beyond a single cluster without added complexity, achieved by extending familiar Kubernetes APIs across clusters and clouds.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: CNCF leadership is explicitly endorsing API-extension over new abstraction as the winning fleet pattern.
insights.quote: Karmada solves this by extending familiar Kubernetes APIs to work across clusters and clouds.

insights.claim: Karmada is one of two CNCF projects that replaced the retired KubeFed (Federation v2); the other, Open Cluster Management, is still in Sandbox and uses a hub-and-spoke agent-based model focused on cluster inventory, add-on APIs, governance and policy distribution, and underpins Red Hat Advanced Cluster Management.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: The successor market has split into a governance/policy camp and a workload-placement camp, and only one has graduated.

insights.claim: Karmada differentiates on workload placement and dynamic scheduling, plus caching layers for cross-cluster resource queries and multi-cluster service discovery, rather than on governance and policy.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Buyers likely need both categories, which implies coexistence rather than a single winner.

insights.claim: The broader competitive set includes Cluster API, which targets cluster lifecycle rather than workload placement, GitOps tools like Argo CD ApplicationSets and Rancher Fleet, and Microsoft's KubeFleet, which is the foundation for Azure Kubernetes Fleet Manager.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Hyperscalers are building proprietary fleet managers on their own open-source bases, so a vendor-neutral graduated project is the main lock-in hedge.
